newsitem.title: UK: N. Irish Protestant prisoners boost peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: N. Irish Protestant prisoners boost peace hopes.

text.p: Convicted Protestant guerrillas gave Northern Ireland's peace hopes a boost on Monday when they backed a shaky two-year-old truce and ruled out retaliation for an IRA bomb attack on a British army base a week ago.
John White of the Ulster Democratic Party, which is close to pro-British Loyalist activists, said after talks with the prisoners that "they are not advocating a return to war".
"I am reassured that they have continued to give their support for a non-return to violence by Loyalist paramilitaries," White told Reuters.

His statement blunted fears that the Loyalists' umbrella organisation, the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), would advocate ending a two-year ceasefire to retaliate for the IRA bomb at the heavily guarded British military headquarters in Northern Ireland last week.

The bombing by the Irish Republican Army was the first in the province for two years and rang alarm bells about a return to the 27-year pattern of retaliatory violence in which about 3,200 people have been killed. The IRA is committed to ending British rule in Northern Ireland.
The CLMC, which groups the outlawed Ulster Defence Association and Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) guerrilla groups, has issued no statement since the bombing at Lisburn, near Belfast.

The views of about 500 Loyalists serving sentences were seen crucial to the reaction of the CLMC, which called a ceasefire two years ago after it received support from within the Maze prison, Northern Ireland's top security jail.
White said the jailed Loyalists believed the IRA and its Sinn Fein political wing were trying to provoke a Loyalist backlash and they decided they would not be sucked back into violence.
"The prisoners recognise that Sinn Fein and the IRA are trying to provoke Loyalists into conflict," he said.
The Irish Independent newspaper, published in Dublin, reported on Monday that the CLMC had agreed to maintain its truce but that further IRA attacks could lead to reprisals.
The paper quoted what it described as a leading loyalist hardliner as saying another IRA attack would be "one too many".

Security sources fear a collapse of the Loyalist truce would result in a resumption of random killings of members of Northern Ireland's Roman Catholic minority, and bombs in Dublin, capital of the Irish Republic.

The UVF sent a message to the Irish government on Monday demanding firm action against the IRA to match the condemnation of both the IRA and Sinn Fein that Irish Prime Minister John Bruton voiced about the attack on the military base.
The message was conveyed by a Dublin peace activist, Chris Hudson, who had a meeting with UVF representatives last week.

Hudson said the Loyalists had noted the heavy security operations mounted by Irish forces to track down the killers of a policeman killed by the IRA earlier this year and a journalist murdered by drug trafficers she was investigating.
"They want to see the government use the Irish security forces to go after the IRA quartermasters in the same way they would go after the drug-barons in Dublin," he said.

Early on Monday Irish security forces arrested three IRA suspects. One was Nessan Quinlivan, who was freed from an Irish jail under a remission scheme earlier this year and is awaiting extradition proceedings to Britain to face charges of escaping from a London jail.
Irish security sources said the three were being questioned about activities in southeastern Ireland.
